terms.whyItMatters: Capital-spending roleplays ask for a quick screen on two equipment quotes, then ask why the faster payback is not automatically the better purchase.

terms.definition: The percentage of a covered cost the policyholder keeps paying after the deductible is met, such as 20% of every bill until an out-of-pocket maximum is reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Health-plan comparison items test that meeting the deductible does not end the client's share of the bill.

terms.definition: A primary key spread across two or more columns, where uniqueness is broken only when every column in the key matches at once — a key on (student_id, course_id) lets the same student appear 6 times and the same course appear 300 times, but the pair exactly once.
terms.whyItMatters: Enrollment and order-line questions ask how many rows one student or one product may hold; the count comes from reading the columns in the key, not from any rule about the table.

terms.definition: Seven-factor analysis the Department of Labor applies to decide whether an unpaid intern is really an employee: who gains the greater benefit, whether the work is tied to academic credit, whether it displaces paid staff, and whether either side expects a paid job at the end. If the employer is the main beneficiary, minimum wage and overtime are owed retroactively.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay staffing a startup with unpaid interns is scored on this test, because failing it turns free labor into back wages.

terms.definition: Comparison of the same line item across periods as a percentage change — current-period amount minus base-period amount, divided by the base-period amount — exposing growth and trend over time, where vertical analysis instead expresses every line as a share of one total within a single period.
terms.whyItMatters: Financial-analysis items give three years of statements and ask which expense category is climbing faster than sales.

terms.definition: The amount a policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance pays anything, and the lever that moves premiums — a higher one lowers the monthly cost and raises the risk carried.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-selection scenarios ask which policy suits a client, and the answer depends on whether they could absorb that first payment in an emergency.

terms.definition: A precomputed lookup of billions of password-to-digest pairs that reverses an unprotected stored password in seconds. Adding a distinct random value to each record before hashing defeats it by arithmetic rather than by secrecy: the attacker must now build one table per record, so 1,000,000 stored passwords demand 1,000,000 tables instead of the single shared one.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why one breached company's passwords were readable overnight and another's were not, the competitor has to explain the per-record work multiplier, not just say the second one 'used encryption'.

terms.definition: Minimum number of members who must be present for a body's votes to count — a majority of the membership under Robert's Rules unless the bylaws set something lower, often one third. Business conducted without one is void rather than merely defeated, so a motion that loses 3 to 2 stands as rejected while the same motion passed short of this number stands as nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A chapter-officer or board roleplay in which half the members skip the meeting is scored on whether the competitor recognizes that no decision can be made.

terms.definition: Direct labor plus manufacturing overhead — the spending required to turn raw materials into finished goods. It deliberately excludes direct materials, which is what separates it from prime cost, defined as direct materials plus direct labor; the two overlap on labor and therefore cannot be added together to reach total product cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost questions ask candidates to sort a list of factory charges into the two groupings, and the shared labor term is where most answers collapse.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring lenders to disclose the annual percentage rate, finance charge and total payments in a standard form before a consumer signs.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why two loan offers in a roleplay can be compared at all, and why a lender quoting only a monthly payment is out of compliance.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: Senior advocate who spends political capital on someone's behalf in rooms that person is not in, putting their name into promotion and staffing decisions and absorbing reputational risk if it goes badly. A mentor spends time instead of capital — advice given directly to you, with nothing of the mentor's own staked on the outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on advancement patterns is scored on this distinction, because the competitor who only asks for coffee chats never gets named in the promotion meeting.

terms.definition: The fixed sequence a period's records travel — analyze source documents, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance, adjust, prepare statements, then close temporary accounts into equity. The order is not optional: statements are drawn before closing, and closing is what resets revenue and expense accounts to zero for the next period.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items present the steps scrambled and ask what comes immediately after the adjusting entries are posted.

terms.definition: A deposit locked for a fixed term at a fixed rate, paying more than a savings account in exchange for a penalty on early withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-vehicle scenarios rule it out for an emergency fund precisely because the money is not reachable without giving up interest.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: Prompt demanding a specific past incident, on the premise that past behavior predicts future behavior, with answers scored against written anchors — which is why a hypothetical answer earns zero. A situational question does the opposite, asking what you would do in a scenario you have never faced, and is scored for reasoning rather than evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: The interview portion of a job-seeking roleplay is graded on giving a dated, quantified incident when the question asks for one, not a description of your general habits.

terms.definition: Estimated total overhead for the coming year divided by the estimated total of an allocation base such as machine hours or direct labor hours, computed before the period begins so jobs can be costed the day they finish. Because both inputs are estimates, actual spending leaves overhead over- or underapplied at year end, and that difference must be closed out.
terms.whyItMatters: Job-costing items ask for the full cost of an order completed in March, long before the year's real overhead is known.

terms.definition: Federal law governing consumer credit files: it grants access to the report, sets who may pull it, and obliges a bureau to investigate a disputed item.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in a roleplay whose report shows an account they never opened has a statutory remedy under it, not just a complaint.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: Cover document sent with an application to a posted opening, naming the requisition and tying two or three of its stated requirements to specific evidence from your record. A letter of inquiry does the same job for a company with no advertised opening, so it opens with the employer's problem instead of with a listing.
terms.whyItMatters: A written-event or job-search roleplay that supplies a job posting expects the letter to answer that posting's requirements point by point.

terms.definition: Overhead assignment that first pools costs by activity — machine setups, inspections, purchase orders — then charges each product using that activity's own cost driver. It corrects the distortion of a single plantwide rate spread on direct labor hours, which systematically overcosts high-volume simple products and undercosts low-volume complex ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost roleplays about a specialty item that looks profitable under the old allocation and loses money under the new one are testing exactly that reversal.

terms.definition: Charging interest above the legal ceiling a state sets, which makes the loan itself unlawful rather than merely expensive.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the legal line separating a high-cost lender from an illegal one in consumer-credit scenarios, and the reason rate caps exist at all.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: The information return a business files for every non-employee it paid $600 or more for services in a calendar year, furnished to both the worker and the IRS by January 31. Nothing is withheld, so the contractor carries the whole 15.3% self-employment tax (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare) and pays it in quarterly estimates, whereas a Form W-2 employee splits that load with an employer paying 7.65%; a payee who supplies no taxpayer ID triggers 24% backup withholding.
terms.whyItMatters: Career-cluster exam items ask what changes when a firm hires a freelance designer instead of a staff one, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays a first-time gig worker is graded on naming the $600 filing trigger and the fact that no tax comes out of the check.

terms.definition: Software running sales, purchasing, inventory, payroll, and accounting off one shared database, so a single shipment posts to inventory, receivables, and the general ledger in one transaction. The gain over separate applications is that nobody re-keys data between them, which removes an entire class of reconciliation errors.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology questions ask why a growing firm outgrows standalone bookkeeping software once its departments each keep their own records.

terms.definition: Money held by a neutral third party until an obligation is met — in a mortgage, the monthly share of property taxes and insurance the lender collects and pays out.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why a mortgage payment exceeds principal and interest in a home-buying scenario, and why it changes when taxes are reassessed.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: Software that parses every application into structured fields and ranks candidates by keyword match against the requisition before a recruiter reads a single one. Multi-column layouts, text inside images and invented section headings are dropped during parsing, so a qualified candidate can be screened out by formatting rather than by qualifications.
terms.whyItMatters: A job-search roleplay advising a competitor whose applications get no response usually turns on this filter, not on the strength of the experience.

terms.definition: A predetermined benchmark for what one unit of input should cost and how much of it should be used, against which actual results are measured. The total gap decomposes into a price variance — actual price minus standard price, times actual quantity — and a quantity variance — actual quantity minus standard quantity, times standard price — so a purchasing decision and a production problem are never blamed on the same manager.
terms.whyItMatters: Manufacturing budget questions supply both actual and standard figures and expect the gap split across the two responsible departments.

terms.definition: A court-supervised liquidation discharging most unsecured debts by selling non-exempt assets, unlike a Chapter 13 filing, which keeps assets under a multi-year repayment plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Debt-control scenarios test that student loans and most taxes survive discharge, and that the filing sits on a credit report for a decade.

terms.definition: The 128-bit addressing scheme succeeding the 32-bit scheme the internet was built on. Because each added bit doubles the space, 128 bits is not four times larger but 2^96 times larger — the older scheme's roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out, and the newer one is written as eight hexadecimal groups rather than four decimal ones.
terms.whyItMatters: An item on the scope of the internet asks why address exhaustion forced a change instead of an expansion; the doubling, not the label, is the explanation.

terms.definition: A route into a second state's professional licence that accepts a licence already held in good standing elsewhere — for CPAs, commonly practice in four of the last ten years plus education and exam requirements the receiving board judges substantially equivalent — instead of requiring the applicant to sit that state's own examination again. It runs one direction only, which is what separates it from reciprocity: the receiving state grants the privilege and the sending state owes nothing in return.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay in which the judge plays an accountant relocating for a promotion turns on whether they must re-test, and exam items on advancement patterns expect this route named rather than a vague 'get licensed again.'

terms.definition: The determination of whether a person is an employee or an independent contractor, made under the IRS common-law control test weighing behavioral control, financial control, and the nature of the relationship. An employee receives a Form W-2 with taxes withheld and the employer's matching payroll tax paid; a contractor receives a Form 1099-NEC and carries the full self-employment tax alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Payroll roleplays about a long-serving contractor who works set hours on company equipment test the control factors and the back-tax exposure of getting them wrong.

terms.definition: The bureau's file of a consumer's accounts, balances and payment history — the underlying record, not the three-digit number calculated from it.
terms.whyItMatters: A client disputing a score in a roleplay has to correct the report first, since the score is only a summary of what the report says.

terms.definition: A 32-bit pattern splitting an address into a network part and a host part: a /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, which is 2^8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are assignable once the network and broadcast addresses come out. A /25 halves that to 126 usable, so borrowing a single bit costs half the room on the segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how many devices a store's network segment can hold, the competitor must convert the slash number into host bits and then subtract 2 — the raw power of two is the wrong answer.

terms.definition: Degree program alternating full-time paid work terms with academic terms, where the work terms carry academic credit and a faculty evaluation. An internship is a single standalone placement with no required academic component, which is why students on this track often graduate with a year or more of documented, evaluated experience.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to build work experience while still in school is scored on distinguishing the credit-bearing alternating program from a one-off summer job.

terms.definition: A projected or adjusted statement built on stated assumptions — next year's forecast, or reported results excluding items management labels non-recurring. It is neither audited nor GAAP, and SEC Regulation G requires a public company publishing any such figure to reconcile it to the nearest GAAP measure so readers can see precisely what was removed.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a startup's projections for a lender, and exam items about a press release touting adjusted earnings, both turn on the unaudited status of this statement.

terms.definition: A court order directing an employer to withhold part of a worker's pay and send it to a creditor, capped by federal law as a share of disposable earnings.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the end point of the debt-control storyline in a personal-finance roleplay, and it reaches the paycheck without the debtor's consent.

terms.definition: Hits divided by total lookups — 900 of 1,000 is 90%. Read as percentage points the figure misleads: moving from 90% to 95% cuts the 100 misses that reach the database down to 50, so a five-point gain halves backend load, and the last few points are worth far more than the first.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks whether a small improvement to a caching layer is worth the spend; the answer runs on misses removed, not on the headline percentage.

terms.definition: Planning credential CFP Board grants to a candidate who holds a bachelor's degree, completes registered coursework, passes a 170-question exam given in two three-hour sessions, and logs 6,000 hours of professional experience — or 4,000 hours under a supervised apprenticeship — then renews with 30 continuing-education hours every two years, 2 of them CFP Board ethics. Against a licence that only obliges a recommendation to be suitable, the difference is the standard of care: the holder must act as a fiduciary and place the client's interest ahead of their own whenever advice is given.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance roleplays that make a competitor explain designations to a client reward the fiduciary-versus-suitability line, and exam items on ongoing education use the 30-hour, two-year renewal as the tested number.

terms.definition: Loan amount divided by the appraised value of the asset securing it; the higher it is, the less cushion a lender has and the more likely mortgage insurance is required.
terms.whyItMatters: Home-financing scenarios test why a larger down payment lowers the cost of borrowing, and this ratio is the mechanism.

terms.definition: The 1,024-based unit an operating system counts in, set against the 1,000-based unit a drive is sold in: a '1 TB' disk holds 10^12 bytes, but the OS divides by 1,024 three times and reports 931 GB — a 7% shortfall that widens at every prefix step, so a 4 TB drive shows as 3.64 TB, roughly 9% short.
terms.whyItMatters: A records-storage item asks how many years of files a purchased drive really holds; sizing the archive off the number on the box overstates capacity before the first backup runs.

terms.definition: The cap a registered apprenticeship program's standards must state under 29 CFR Part 29 on how many apprentices may work per experienced worker on a job — one to one is the common floor, and a sponsor that exceeds its registered figure risks deregistration of the whole program. It travels with a stepped wage schedule: the apprentice begins near 50% of the journeyworker rate and moves up at fixed hour milestones, so the sponsor's cost per apprentice climbs across the term rather than staying flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how a small contractor can afford to train new workers is answered with the supervision ratio and the stepped percentage, and exam items pair it with registered apprenticeship to test whether the competitor knows the arrangement is federally regulated rather than an informal handshake.

terms.definition: A spreadsheet address locking exactly one of the two coordinates — $B5 pins the column and lets the row travel, B$5 does the reverse. Filling a multiplication grid both across and down needs one of each inside the same formula ($B5*C$4); pinning both coordinates or neither returns a wrong value in every cell except the one it was typed into.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items grade the filled grid rather than the first cell, so a formula that is correct where it is written and wrong everywhere it is dragged scores zero.

terms.term: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act
terms.definition: Federal statute obliging an employer of 100 or more employees to give 60 calendar days' written notice before a plant closing that ends 50 or more jobs at one site within any 30-day window, or a mass layoff of 500 workers — or of 50 to 499 when that reaches a third of the site's active workforce. Skipping notice is not a fine paid to the government: the remedy is back pay and benefits owed to each affected worker for every day of shortfall, capped at 60.
terms.whyItMatters: Worker-rights exam items use the 60-day count to kill distractors, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays an employee hearing closing rumors is scored on stating the notice entitlement and the back-pay remedy instead of offering reassurance.

terms.definition: An employer rule capping what any manager may tell a reference checker — dates of employment, job title, and sometimes final pay — adopted because a former employer's comment on performance holds its qualified privilege only while made in good faith and loses it, opening a defamation claim, once malice or reckless falsehood is shown. It is not a universal shield: a handful of states run service-letter statutes, Missouri's being the model, that compel a letter stating the cause of separation within 45 days of a certified-mail request from anyone who worked at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: Professional-development roleplays hand the competitor a manager who wants to warn another firm about a fired employee, and the graded answer is the disclosure limit plus the legal reason for it; job-search exam items use the same rule to explain why a former supervisor will confirm only dates.

terms.definition: A legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law roleplays turn on whether promises, rights, and duties are enforceable.

terms.definition: Giving full attention, checking understanding, and responding thoughtfully to a speaker.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect competitors to handle questions and concerns clearly.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: The function that recruits, develops, and manages employees to meet organizational goals.
terms.whyItMatters: HR decisions shape staffing quality, service delivery, and culture.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: A formal document requesting goods or services from a vendor at set terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchase orders create the paper trail for efficient procurement.

terms.definition: A growth grid crossing products (existing vs. new) with markets (existing vs. new) to produce four moves — market penetration, market development, product development, and diversification — ordered from lowest to highest risk because each new axis adds unfamiliar variables.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks how a regional chain should grow next year is answered by naming the specific Ansoff cell and its risk level, not by saying 'expand'.

terms.definition: Something of value exchanged between parties that makes a contract binding.
terms.whyItMatters: Without consideration, an agreement is a mere promise and not legally enforceable.

terms.definition: A readability score that converts a passage into a U.S. school grade: 0.39 x (total words / total sentences) + 11.8 x (total syllables / total words) - 15.59. Because sentence length is multiplied by 0.39 and syllable count by 11.8, swapping 'utilize' for 'use' moves the score less than splitting one 30-word sentence into two 15-word ones; consumer-facing documents are normally targeted at grade 8 or below.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to rewrite a return policy for shoppers is scored on whether you can name a measurable target and the two levers that hit it, instead of promising to 'make it simpler.'

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: (All external recruiting costs + all internal recruiting costs) divided by the number of hires made in the same period — advertising, agency fees, travel, referral bonuses and recruiter salary all belong in the numerator, so $84,000 of total spend against 24 hires is $3,500. Only completed hires count in the denominator, never openings still in process.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring-manager roleplay that asks you to justify a recruiting budget to an owner is scored on whether you divide total recruiting spend by hires rather than quoting the job-board invoice alone.
